opus-5.5.text:
I think the analogy is about the stage a field is in, not about how advanced it is.

Look at physics in the 1700s. People had powerful tools. Newtonian mechanics worked incredibly well, and you could predict planetary orbits and build machines. But many of the deeper concepts weren't there yet. Energy wasn't a unified idea. Thermodynamics didn't exist as a theory. Electricity and magnetism were mostly a collection of fascinating experiments. People rubbed glass rods, made Leyden jars, and saw sparks. They were accumulating phenomena faster than they could explain them.

AI feels very similar to me right now. We have something that works astonishingly well. You scale up a transformer, train it on enough data, add reinforcement learning, and capabilities emerge. We have empirical regularities like scaling laws, which feel a bit like Kepler's laws. They're precise and useful, but they're descriptive. They tell you *what* happens, not really *why*. We don't have the equivalent of a Maxwell or a Boltzmann yet, someone who tells us what the right underlying quantities even are. What is "intelligence," measured properly? What is a model actually learning when its loss goes down? Why does generalization happen where it does?

So a lot of the best work today is experimental, almost like natural philosophy. You try things, you observe carefully, and you build intuition. Good researchers right now are often people with very good taste about which experiments to run, rather than people deriving things from first principles, because the first principles aren't written down yet.

There's another part of the analogy I find exciting. In eighteenth-century physics, a single person or a small group could still discover something fundamental. The field wasn't fully carved up. I think AI is like that now. The low-hanging fruit is still everywhere, and the conceptual framework is still being formed. Fifty or a hundred years from now, people may look back at our papers the way we look at early experiments on electricity: they were clearly onto something real, but they didn't yet have the language for it.

For me, that also means some humility. A lot of what we confidently say today about why things work will probably turn out to be wrong or at least naive. The phenomena are real, but our explanations are provisional.

r001.rationale: The response compares AI’s empirical experimentation and incomplete theoretical framework to eighteenth-century physics, but it does not identify combining theory and experiment within the same researcher’s work as the basis of the comparison.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the analogy comes from how empirical the field is right now. In the eighteenth century, before thermodynamics was really worked out, people built steam engines that worked, and they got better and better at building them, but nobody could tell you precisely why they worked. The theory came after the engineering. Carnot and the others were basically trying to explain machines that already existed.

That's very much where we are with AI. We have scaling laws, we have these huge models that clearly do something remarkable, and the people training them have a lot of intuition and recipes. But if you ask a deep question, like why does reinforcement learning on language models generalize in the way it does, or why does pre-training produce priors that make RL work so well, the honest answer is that we don't really have a theory. We have experiments, and we have a lot of folk wisdom.

I actually think that's a good thing to recognize, because it tells you what kind of research matters. In a period like that, careful experiments matter a lot, and so does getting the right concepts. Thermodynamics didn't come from more clever engines, it came from someone asking the right abstract question about heat and work. For AI, I think the analogous questions are about things like what an environment is, what generalization means for an agent, and how experience should be turned into learning. We're at the stage where defining the problems well is probably more valuable than any single new method.

The other thing the analogy captures is the sense of possibility. Eighteenth-century physicists weren't embarrassed that they lacked a full theory. They were excited, because it was obvious the phenomena were real and important. I feel the same way. It can be uncomfortable to work in a field where so much is empirical, but it also means the foundational ideas are still up for grabs.

r001.rationale: The response compares AI’s empirical progress and lack of theory with eighteenth-century engineering, but does not identify theory and experiment being integrated within the same researcher’s work.

astra-6.text:
I think the resemblance is that our ability to observe and build things is ahead of our ability to explain them. In eighteenth-century physics, people could discover interesting phenomena and formulate useful laws without having a unified picture of what was happening. AI feels a little like that today. We can train a model and see remarkable capabilities, but we don’t have a theory that reliably predicts which capabilities will emerge or why a particular approach works better.

That makes experimentation very important. But a good experiment should do more than produce a higher benchmark score—it should help us distinguish between explanations. If a model fails at a task, is it missing knowledge? Is it unable to reason through the problem? Or does it need a better way to interact with its environment? Those lead to different research directions.

So I see this as an exciting stage: there are useful systems to build, but also basic concepts that haven’t been settled. The opportunity is to move back and forth between the two—to let building reveal the questions, and let scientific investigation guide what we build next.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the resemblance is that we can observe a lot of interesting phenomena, but we don’t yet have a unified theory that explains them. We can build increasingly capable models, measure their behavior, and discover empirical regularities, but our ability to explain or predict what happens is still limited.

In that sense, AI research feels like physics before its foundations were fully established. You need experiments, good instruments, and the right questions. Sometimes a surprising observation is more valuable than a beautiful theory, because it tells you that your current picture is incomplete.

That’s also what makes this period exciting. There’s room for people who build systems, people who study their behavior, and people who try to turn those observations into principles. The challenge is to connect those activities—to make experiments that teach us something, rather than simply produce a higher benchmark score.

r001.rationale: The response says AI research needs experiments and theory, and calls for connecting those activities, but does not identify integrating theory and experiment within the same researcher’s work as the basis of the comparison.
